title: Protocol for cortical-wide field-of-view two-photon imaging with quick neonatal adeno-associated virus injection
protocol: Inject into the planned area indicated in gray with a red square representing the two-photon imaging zone.
Ensure the glass pipette tip stops in the middle of the cortical layer during injection to allow dye to spread throughout the cortex.
Avoid injecting too deeply, as this can cause the pipette tip to reach the lateral ventricles and lead to rapid dye dispersion.
Prevent shallow injections that do not penetrate the cortical layer, causing dye accumulation between the skin and brain tissue.
Thaw the tube of AAV stock on ice.
Dilute AAV with saline or PBS solution.
Add 0.1% (w/v) Fast Green FCF to the AAV solution.
Maintain the AAV solution on ice until use.
Prepare an ice bed filled with ice and covered with aluminum foil.
Set the polished glass pipette to the micromanipulator.
Connect the pipette and a 5-mL syringe with Tygon laboratory tubing.
Bring pups to the working space.
Prepare a recovery box with bedding.
Take half the number of pups from their mother and place them into the recovery box.
Place the recovery box onto the heating mat.
Anesthetize a pup by laying it on top of the ice bed for 1–2 min until it does not move.
Load 4.1–4.2 μL of AAV solution into the glass pipette using a syringe.
Place the head of the anesthetized pup in a head holder to inject the pipette perpendicular to the cortical layer.
Rotate the pup’s head slightly in the head holder so that the injection point is facing up.
Set the pipette perpendicular to the cortical layer.
Monitor the depth of the injection point accurately.
Insert the pipette tip to the surface of the injection point.
Manually inject AAV into the cortex.
Insert the glass pipette 280–300 μm deep from the surface.
Critical: Ensure the injection depth is optimal for dye/AAV spread throughout the cortex.
Monitor for dye spread in a crescent formation indicating too deep an injection.
Observe for AAV solution accumulation and skin swelling indicating too shallow an injection.
Manually inject 4 μL of AAV solution into the cortex at a speed of 4 μL/min by slowly pushing the syringe.
Check if the injection depth is correct by observing the spread of the green dye after the first shot.
If the dye forms a small dot at the injection site, proceed with the second shot.
Adjust the injection depth to ensure a small dot of dye appears after injecting a small amount of AAV solution.
Perform the second shot with 3–4 μL of AAV solution.
Observe that the dye spreads slowly throughout the hemisphere without leaking into the opposite hemisphere.
Inject 4 μL AAV solution per animal for consistent cortical-wide expression.
Withdraw the glass pipette from the brain.
Recover the pups and place them inside the recovery box on top of a heating mat.
Repeat injection procedure for each pup in the recovery box.
Gently return injected pups to their mother with the bedding.
Check the temperature of the pups before returning them to their mother.
Anesthetize mice with 0.5–2% isoflurane.
Set the mouse to the head holder and expose the skull.
Shave hair and clean the skin with 70% EtOH.
Spray local anesthetic to the skin.
Cut the scalp and expose the skull.
Attach the cut scalp to the left and right sides with surgical tape.
Observe the sensor fluorescence with fluorescent microscopy.
Apply saline to prevent drying after exposing the skull.
Place a φ22 mm coverslip on the observation area.
Set the mouse under fluorescent microscopy.
Observe the green fluorescence with blue light.
Note the presence and distribution of green fluorescence throughout the hemisphere.
Record fluorescence intensities under different conditions during macro-imaging.
Determine optimal macro-imaging conditions retrospectively from two-photon imaging results.
Confirm sufficient brightness and appropriate expression level of green fluorescence.
Stitch up the skin.
Recover the mouse.
Wait for a predetermined time to allow the animals to grow for craniotomy.
Implant double coverslips and a head plate to allow two-photon imaging.
Perform surgical operation of implantation following previously reported protocols.
Anesthetize the mouse with an anesthetic of choice (e.g., isoflurane).
Administer antibiotic enrofloxacin (5 μg/g body weight) via subcutaneous injection.
Create a cranial window large enough for the FOV of the two-photon microscopy.
Set the head of the mouse in the head holder.
Shave hair from the surgical site and clean the skin with 70% EtOH.
Cover the eyes of the mouse with cream to prevent dryness.
Apply a topical anesthetic to the skin.
Cut the skin and expose the skull.
Clean the exposed skull with a dental etching liquid.
Gently scratch the surface of the skull along the cranial hole using a Bonn Micro Probe, a fine needle.
Drill a groove along the mark using a drill at 1000–5000 rpm.
Remove small bone fragments or dust generated during drilling using air duster or suction.
Gently remove the island of the grooved skull by lifting it with fine forceps.
Apply NRR to the groove and to the surface of the brain tissue constantly.
Expose the dura mater after detaching it from the skull.
If bleeding occurs, rinse the surface of the dura with the NRR solution until it stops.
Rinse the surface of the brain tissue with NRR.
Keep the surface of the brain tissue moist by applying NRR constantly.
Remove the exposed dura mater with fine forceps.
Implant the double coverslip on the skull surface.
Rinse the surface of the brain tissue and the double coverslip with NRR.
Place the smaller coverslip into the cranial hole in contact with the brain surface.
Push the coverslip slightly to ensure adherence of the brain tissue to the small coverslip side.
Apply a thin layer of cyanoacrylate adhesive between the edge of the larger coverslip and the edge of the cranial hole.
Allow the cyanoacrylate adhesive to dry for approximately 5 minutes.
Seal the double coverslip to the skull using dental cement, covering the edges of the larger coverslip.
Allow the dental cement to cure.
Mix 15 mM sterile HCl with human recombinant leptin.
Expose the skull and scratch its surface along the cranial hole using a fine needle.
Gently drill a cranial hole along the mark and remove the dura mater, covering the brain tissue with NRR.
Place and fix the double coverslip into the cranial hole.
Apply a thin layer of cyanoacrylate adhesive between the edge of the larger coverslip and the skull edge.
Fix the double coverslips to the skull using dental cement solution.
Place and fix a stainless head plate horizontal to the surface of the coverslips using dental cement.
Apply dental cement to entirely cover the exposed skull, wound margins, and edges of the dental cement used to fix the coverslips and the head plate.
Allow the dental cement to fully cure.
